## Less friction. More possibility.

**Find the need. Build on evidence. Open it to everyone.**

<details>
<summary><strong>Two sets of ten principles for useful tools</strong></summary>

When a need is misunderstood, even a sophisticated feature can struggle to find a use. When a needed feature is slow or unreliable, that usefulness is hard to sustain. I therefore set out **what I build for** in “Ten Principles for User Value” and **how I protect that value** in “Yeony’s Ten Development Principles.” These are the criteria I want to revisit whenever I add a feature or change direction.

### Ten Principles for User Value

These principles begin with people’s needs and aim for outcomes that actually help.

#### 01. I build things for others to use, not just for myself.

**Reason and basis** — A way of working that feels familiar to its maker will not necessarily feel natural to a first-time user. Convenience for me alone does not tell me whether a tool will help someone else’s work.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to begin by asking who will seek out this tool, in what situation, and to finish what task. Following that person’s workflow from opening it to taking away a result can bring it closer to a tool they return to when they need it.

#### 02. I build things that did not exist before.

**Reason and basis** — Even among existing tools, there may be unresolved tasks or disconnected workflows. I believe those gaps can provide a reason to make something new.

**Choice and expectation** — I aim to connect scattered steps or bring in methods from other fields to make previously difficult work possible. When people can actually do more, novelty gains a clear purpose.

#### 03. I build for creation rather than consumption.

**Reason and basis** — When time and attention leave behind an output or a learned method, they can carry into the next task. I want one use of a tool to become a stepping stone to the next attempt.

**Choice and expectation** — I value workflows that let people make, revise, compare, save, and reuse their results. If something remains in their hands after using a tool, I hope their ability to do things for themselves will gradually expand.

#### 04. I reduce the waste that repeated small inconveniences create.

**Reason and basis** — Moving files or entering the same values again may seem minor once, but repetition consumes time and attention. I believe an inconvenience should be judged by both the effort of one occurrence and how often it recurs.

**Choice and expectation** — I aim to group frequently repeated steps and reduce requests for information already provided. Less effort spent on preparation and cleanup leaves more room for judgment and creativity.

#### 05. I question inconveniences we have come to accept.

**Reason and basis** — Long-established workflows can mix essential steps with steps left over from past constraints. Familiarity alone does not tell us whether a step is still necessary.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to ask, “Why must we take this step?” and check whether its reason still applies today. Finding where constraints have changed can make it possible to remove steps, beyond simply explaining them more clearly.

#### 06. I value needs shared by only a few people.

**Reason and basis** — The number of users and the depth of one person’s difficulty are different measures. Even if few people need a tool, the lack of a suitable alternative can make one small tool the difference between possible and impossible work.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to consider how specific the need is, how severe the difficulty is, and whether other solutions exist. I believe development also has value when it gives people with few options a practical way forward.

#### 07. I understand the real purpose behind a user’s request.

**Reason and basis** — “Please add a button” may mean wanting fewer steps or a clearer way to check a result. Looking only at the proposed feature can hide the problem it is meant to solve.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to understand the situation behind a request and the desired outcome first, then find a fitting solution. A clearer purpose helps me choose the right features and reduce people’s effort more directly.

#### 08. I listen to the people who actually use what I build.

**Reason and basis** — The workflow I imagine during development may differ from what happens in real environments. Where people stop and what they struggle to understand must be checked through actual use.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to listen to the context behind feedback and the points where people get stuck, then check whether a change has resolved the issue. Repeating this process can narrow the gap between my expectations and real use and clarify which improvements come first.

#### 09. I make complex technology easy for anyone to use.

**Reason and basis** — If people must learn difficult terminology and settings before reaching a feature, its benefits reach only those who cross that threshold. I need to distinguish what the user must understand from what the tool can handle for them.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to prioritize clear language about purpose, sensible defaults for the situation, and feedback that makes results checkable. Fine controls should be available when needed, so beginners can start and experienced users can go deeper.

#### 10. I build things that are useful in practice.

**Reason and basis** — A feature’s usefulness can be seen in how easily it helps someone complete real work. If input is cumbersome or results are hard to understand and take away, its benefit diminishes at that point.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to examine accuracy, clarity, and effort from the first step through using the result. If people can move naturally into their next task, the usefulness that motivated development can be confirmed in practice.

### Yeony’s Ten Development Principles

These are the standards I want to uphold so needed features work reliably across environments and can keep improving over time.

#### 01. I can explain why each feature needs to exist.

**Reason and basis** — Adding a feature expands not only implementation work, but also what users must understand and what must be maintained. When its benefit is unclear, it is hard to justify the complexity it adds.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to define the problem each feature solves, when it is needed, and how to judge whether it works well. A clear reason for its existence helps prioritize additions and revisions and keeps the tool’s purpose consistent.

#### 02. I build with logic grounded in evidence.

**Reason and basis** — Choosing a familiar method or a plausible-looking result alone makes it difficult to explain when it works well. Both the underlying mechanism and observed results are needed to assess a choice.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to explain the connection between the problem, the chosen method, and the results I checked. Making the basis of a decision visible helps correct poor choices and identify where to begin the next improvement.

#### 03. I distinguish assumptions from verified facts.

**Reason and basis** — Treating an untested premise as fact carries the same uncertainty into later decisions. For analysis and estimation in particular, the conditions and extent of verification matter.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to separate what is known, what is estimated, and what still needs checking, and state the scope of verification. This gives users a basis for interpreting results and helps me see the next question to investigate.

#### 04. I connect knowledge across fields to open new possibilities.

**Reason and basis** — Different fields may face similar problems in measuring change, finding patterns, and controlling outcomes. A method learned in one field may offer a way through an obstacle in another.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to connect knowledge from photography, audio, and interfaces while checking that a borrowed method remains valid under its new conditions. I hope these connections can join separate features into one workflow and open new ways of creating.

#### 05. I keep processing on the user’s device whenever possible.

**Reason and basis** — Sending files elsewhere adds transfer time and network dependence. When a task can be completed on the device, there is an opportunity to design a workflow without transmitting the originals.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to finish as much processing locally as the workload and device capabilities allow, and clearly state where files are processed. I hope to reduce unnecessary transfers and give people more direct control over their work and data.

#### 06. I deliver the needed performance with minimal resources.

**Reason and basis** — Devices differ in processing power, memory, and screen size, so a resource-heavy design can narrow the environments where a tool is usable. Supporting many devices means considering both access and the burden of actual operation.

**Choice and expectation** — I build for the web to lower operating-system barriers, **make responsive design a foundation, and optimize performance as far as possible.** Guided by the quality and responsiveness needed, I aim to reduce unnecessary computation and memory use so the tool stays useful on small screens and limited hardware.

#### 07. I plan for external services to become unavailable.

**Reason and basis** — An external service’s availability and delivery model are outside my control. If a single dependency stops an entire task, the user’s workflow can stop with it.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to examine core dependencies and design fallback paths, clear interruption status, and ways to preserve work in progress. Limiting the impact and making recovery clear helps people choose their next action during an interruption.

#### 08. I make results comparable and reproducible.

**Reason and basis** — When inputs or settings differ, it is difficult to tell whether a result changed because of an improvement or because of other conditions. Keeping the comparison conditions helps narrow down the cause.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to record inputs, settings, versions, and other factors that affect results, so they can be checked again under the same conditions. Comparison and reproduction make tracing problems and verifying the effects of changes more precise.

#### 09. I clearly disclose limitations and known issues.

**Reason and basis** — To use results appropriately, people need to know both the conditions where a tool works well and those requiring careful interpretation. Without visible limits, it is hard to judge how far to trust a result.

**Choice and expectation** — I want to explain supported scope, known issues, and where results are estimates at the points where that information is needed. Helping people judge fitness for their purpose and double-check results when necessary is a basis for trust.

#### 10. I build so the work can be maintained and improved over time.

**Reason and basis** — Tools need changes as environments and needs evolve. If their structure and the reasons behind choices are hard to understand, even small changes take time and needed improvements can be delayed.

**Choice and expectation** — I want clear responsibilities in the structure, records of why choices were made, and ways to check the effects of changes. If my future self and others working on the tool can understand it more easily, we have a better chance of fixing problems and keeping it useful.

</details>
